questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent to a Trajectory Given an Initial Value Problem
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(1,-2)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(1,-2)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =2x-2y \\  & =2(1)-2(-2) \\  & =6 \\ {y}^{′} & =2x-3y \\  & =2(1)-3(-2) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent to a Trajectory Given an Initial Value Problem
questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}],\,x(t)={e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+9[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -36\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -36\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -36\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(-1)(\frac{2}{3})+0(-36) \\ 0\cdot (\frac{2}{3})+2(-36)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -72\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(3,-1)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(3,-1)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =-x+4y \\  & =-3+4(-1) \\  & =-3-4 \\  & =-7 \\ {y}^{′} & =2x+2y \\  & =2(3)+2(-1) \\  & =6-2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 4\end{aligned}].

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(1,-1)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(1,-1)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$

$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & ={e}^{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{3(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Nullclines of a System of Differential Equation
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.

$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
2x+4y=0\,⇒\,y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
-x+y=0\,⇒\,y=x
$$

Plotting these in the phase space, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068646/assets/59a731b27e2333fef2bfa48e9e61a7075548ddd74782c1fadf1dd98f68ef2a7e.png)

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068646/assets/d8be54eddd0358742170a03b3c55e0cb94eaf2a7d59f12e1c4361a6197d29847.png)
Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\ln 2?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\ln 2$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & ={e}^{3(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+2\cdot 2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(12)+1(4) \\ 1(12)+2(4)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}24+4 \\ 12+8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which $x' = 0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0{:}$

$$
3x-y=0 
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
y = 3x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which $y' = 0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0{:}$

$$
-2x-y=0 
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
y = -2x
$$

Plotting these in the phase space, we obtain the following:
